questions.question: In which city was David Gans born?
questions.explanation: He was born in 1541 to a family of moneylenders, and first studied in Bonn and Frankfurt.

questions.question: Which of his teachers "raised and exalted" him and initiated him into the secret of the sciences?
questions.explanation: The Rema incorporated philosophy and astronomy into his writings, and under his patronage Gans was exposed to Euclid in Hebrew translation.

questions.question: In which year did Gans publish "Tzemach David"?
questions.explanation: In the Hebrew year 5352. The Frankfurt edition (1692) added a third part to it.

questions.question: How is "Tzemach David" divided?
options: According to the tractates of the Talmud
According to the countries of the Diaspora
According to the sefirot of Kabbalah
The history of Israel, and in a separate part the history of the nations
questions.explanation: The division reflects a distinction between the sacred history of Israel and general history.

questions.question: True or false: Gans based the second part of "Tzemach David" on Jewish sources only.
questions.explanation: This was the first serious attempt by an Ashkenazi Jew to encompass world history, and in it he cited Christian authors.

questions.question: True or false: "Tzemach David" was the standard history book in Jewish homes in Ashkenaz until the 19th century.
questions.explanation: The book gave Ashkenazi Jewry its first historical awareness.

questions.question: True or false: Gans spent three days at the observatory of Tycho Brahe.
questions.explanation: In Benátky, in the castle of Emperor Rudolf II. He took part in observations and described the instruments with excitement.

questions.question: What task did Tycho Brahe assign to Gans?
options: To translate the "Alfonsine Tables" from Hebrew into German
To calculate the molad of the moon for the Emperor
To build him an observation instrument
questions.explanation: The tables were essential for calculating the positions of the stars, and Brahe recognized Gans's access to the Jewish-Sephardic scientific tradition.

questions.question: Whom did Gans meet at Tycho Brahe's, as Brahe's assistant?
questions.explanation: Prague in the late 16th century was the capital of world astronomy.

questions.question: In which book did Gans deal with astronomy?
questions.explanation: The book was written around 1612 and printed only in 1743. In it he set out all the astronomical and geographical knowledge of his time.

questions.question: Which astronomical model did Gans prefer?
options: Copernicus's: the sun at the center
A model in which the earth is flat
Tycho Brahe's: the earth at the center, and the planets revolve around the sun
questions.explanation: He was the first Jew to mention Copernicus by name, and called him "a wondrous sage without equal," but did not accept his system.

questions.question: True or false: Gans described the discovery of America and the sphericity of the earth.
questions.explanation: He was among the first in Ashkenazi Jewry to do so, and claimed that science only confirms what the sages of Israel knew.

questions.question: What does the name "Gans" mean, which he hinted at in the signature "David Avzi"?
questions.explanation: On his tombstone in the old cemetery in Prague a Star of David and a goose are engraved.

questions.question: According to Gans, from where did the science of the stars reach the Greeks?
options: From the Babylonians, who discovered it themselves
From the Egyptians, who learned it from the forefathers of Israel
questions.explanation: Therefore engaging in science is not the adoption of a foreign culture, but the "return of a lost object" of a Jewish wisdom that was forgotten in exile.

questions.question: True or false: Gans was a community rabbi and composed many books of responsa.
questions.explanation: He was not a community rabbi and did not compose responsa or pilpul, and yet his influence on Jewish culture was far-reaching.

questions.question: True or false: Gans wrote his books for sages only, in scholarly Hebrew.
questions.explanation: He wrote in Yiddish and in simple Hebrew, also for householders and for the young, in order to make the knowledge accessible to the public.

questions.question: On what did Gans base the permission to read the second part of "Tzemach David" on Shabbat?
options: On a responsum of the Maharal, who permitted every book
On the rule that there is no prohibition against reading on Shabbat
On the ruling of the Rema, which permits books of chronicles that contain moral teaching
On the fact that the book was written in Yiddish
questions.explanation: The Rema in Orach Chayim, section 307. His other reasons: moral lessons, good relations with the neighbors and strengthening of faith.

questions.question: What were Gans's reasons for rejecting Copernicus's system?
options: Copernicus was not a good mathematician
The Maharal forbade him to engage in this
Brahe's model explained the observations and did not directly contradict the plain sense of Scripture
questions.explanation: He also argued that the heliocentric system is not new, and that it originates with Pythagoras and his school.

questions.question: What is the "Irenism" that scholarship attributes to Gans?
options: An aspiration for reconciliation between religions through shared scientific knowledge
A preference for history over Talmud
A belief that science will replace religion
questions.explanation: He saw astronomy as a "theologically neutral" domain, a bridge on which Jews and Christians would respect one another.

questions.question: Which separation, which he learned from the Maharal and the Rema, reduced, according to the research, the friction between science and faith?
options: Science is permitted only to mature sages
Science deals only with the laws of nature, not with the essence of God or the reasons for the commandments
Science is studied only in a foreign language
Science deals with the heavens and Torah with the earth
questions.explanation: Thus he could see in the beit midrash and in the observatory two places in which divine truth is revealed.
